text: American Express Company, a globally integrated payments company founded in 1850 and incorporated in 1965 as a New York corporation, operates as a bank holding company under the Bank Holding Company Act of 1956, as amended, and is subject to supervision and examination by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The company provides credit and charge cards to consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations worldwide through its various products and services, available via mobile and online applications, affiliate marketing, customer referral programs, third-party service providers, direct mail, telephone, in-house sales teams, and direct response advertising. Its businesses are organized into four reportable operating segments: U.S. Consumer Services (USCS), Commercial Services (CS), International Card Services (ICS), and Global Merchant and Network Services (GMNS), with corporate functions and certain other businesses included in Corporate & Other. The company’s end-to-end integrated payments platform connects Card Members and merchants through direct relationships, enabling access to spending data for risk underwriting, fraud reduction, and targeted marketing, while protecting data in compliance with applicable policies and laws. It also obtains data through contractual relationships with third-party card issuers, merchant acquirers, aggregators, and processors. The company’s global proprietary card-issuing businesses are conducted through USCS, CS, and ICS, offering a broad range of card products, rewards, and services to consumers and commercial customers, with a focus on attracting Millennial and Gen Z customers and expanding SME offerings through products like business checking and consumer rewards checking, as well as digital capabilities from acquisitions of Kabbage, Resy, and acompay. The ICS organization consolidates consumer, SME, and large commercial card issuing activities outside the U.S. to better serve local priorities, with significant billed business in the United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, Japan, Canada, and Mexico. For the fiscal year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide billed business (spending on American Express cards issued by the company) was $1,338 billion, and the company had 76.7 million proprietary cards-in-force worldwide. The GMNS segment manages relationships with millions of merchants globally, including signing new merchants, setting discount rates, and handling merchant servicing, and operates through programs like OptBlue® that allow third-party acquirers to contract directly with small merchants. The company also provides fraud-prevention tools, marketing solutions, and data analytics to merchants and partners. Through its card network, American Express operates in approximately 103 countries and territories, licensing the American Express brand to third-party banks and institutions to issue local currency cards and serve as merchant acquirers. For the year ended December 31, 2022, worldwide network services processed volume (spending on American Express cards issued by third parties) was $214.5 billion, and the company had 56.5 million cards-in-force issued by third parties worldwide. The company’s diverse customer base includes consumers, small businesses, mid-sized companies, and large corporations, with a global footprint supported by partnerships. Key partners include Delta Air Lines, Marriott International, Hilton Worldwide Holdings, British Airways, Amazon.com (via Pay with Points), PayPal, i2c, BILL, BillTrust, Versapay, and Fine Hotels and Resorts. Delta is the company’s largest strategic partner, with the Delta cobrand portfolio representing approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. The Delta cobrand portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards, with the current agreement running through the end of 2029 and the company planning significant investments in the partnership. Delta also participates in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits such as airport lounge access, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and serves as a corporate payments customer. The company’s spend-centric business model generates revenue primarily by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. As of June 30, 2022, the aggregate market value of the registrant’s voting shares held by non-affiliates was approximately $104.0 billion based on the closing sale price on the New York Stock Exchange. As of February 2, 2023, there were 744,192,702 common shares outstanding. The company is a well-known seasoned issuer and has filed all required reports under Section 13 or 15(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 during the preceding 12 months and has been subject to such filing requirements for the past 90 days. It has submitted electronically every Interactive Data File required under Rule 405 of Regulation S-T and is classified as a large accelerated filer. The registrant has filed a report on and attestation to its management’s assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting under Section 404(b) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. The terms “American Express,” “we,” “our,” or “us” refer to American Express Company and its subsidiaries on a consolidated basis unless otherwise stated or implied. The use of the term “partner” or “partnering” does not imply a formal legal partnership and does not alter the terms of American Express’ relationship with third parties.

Revenues and expenses related to Delta are significant and represent a major source of value for American Express Card Members. The Delta cobrand portfolio accounted for approximately 10 percent of worldwide network volumes and about 21 percent of worldwide Card Member loans as of December 31, 2022. This portfolio generates fee revenue and interest income from Card Members and discount revenue from Delta and other merchants for spending on Delta cobrand cards. The current Delta cobrand agreement extends through the end of 2029, and the company expects to continue making significant investments in this partnership. Delta is also a key participant in the Membership Rewards program, provides travel-related benefits and services including airport lounge access for certain American Express Card Members, accepts American Express cards as a merchant, and is a corporate payments customer. American Express works with all partners to deliver value, choice, and unique experiences to its customer base. The company’s “spend-centric” business model primarily generates revenue by driving spending on its cards and secondarily through finance charges and fees. Spending on American Express cards is, on average, higher per card than that of competitors, offering merchants loyal customers and larger transactions, which in turn enables the company to invest in attractive rewards, targeted marketing, and other programs for both Card Members and merchants. This model differentiates American Express cards and provides value to Card Members, merchants, and business partners. The American Express brand, known for trust, security, and service, is among the most valuable globally and is protected through extensive investment in trademarks, service marks, and patents worldwide. The company aims to deliver the world’s best customer experience daily, with its reputation for service recognized through numerous awards. Customer care professionals, travel consultants, and partners are trained to enhance the brand experience and deepen customer relationships. American Express focuses on four strategic imperatives: expanding leadership in the premium consumer space by offering benefits across everyday spending, borrowing, travel, and lifestyle needs, expanding global business partnerships, and creating experiences that attract high-spending customers; building on its strong position in commercial payments by evolving card value propositions, differentiating corporate card and accounts payable solutions, and introducing innovative financing, banking, and payment products for business customers; strengthening its global, integrated network by increasing merchant acceptance, providing fraud protection, marketing insights, and connections to high-spending Card Members, and collaborating with network partners to expand offerings; and leveraging its unique global position to support its other strategic goals. Previously, a strategic imperative to make American Express an essential part of customers’ digital lives has become embedded in the company’s operations. The company also has an Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) strategy with three pillars: promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion (DE&I) to foster a diverse, equitable, and inclusive workforce and society; advancing climate solutions by enhancing operations to meet customer and community needs in a low-carbon future; and building financial confidence by offering responsible, secure, and transparent products and services to help individuals and businesses achieve financial resilience. The company emphasizes a culture built on supportive relationships and inclusivity, where colleagues feel welcome, heard, and supported in their growth. This culture is guided by the Blue Box Values: We Do What's Right, We Embrace Diversity, We Back Our Customers, We Stand for Equity and Inclusion, We Make It Great, We Win as a Team, We Respect People, and We Support Communities. As of December 31, 2022, American Express employed approximately 77,300 colleagues, with about 26,000 in the United States and 51,300 outside the United States. The company added colleagues in 2022 to support business growth. To attract and retain top talent, it offers competitive compensation and leading benefits and invests in programs such as on-the-job learning tools, cross-border assignments, career coaching, mentoring, rotation opportunities, virtual learning, and formal classroom instruction. The health and wellness of colleagues is a priority, with a holistic approach addressing physical, financial, and mental well-being. In 2022, the company launched Amex Flex, allowing colleagues to work in the office, at home, or in a hybrid model based on role and business needs, to broaden the talent pool and improve retention. An annual Colleague Experience Survey showed that 92 percent of participating colleagues would recommend American Express as a great place to work. The 2022 company scorecard included talent retention, colleague engagement, and diversity representation goals. As of December 31, 2022, women made up 53.7 percent of the global workforce, and in the U.S. workforce, Asian, Black/African American, and Hispanic/Latinx colleagues represented 18.7 percent, 17.9 percent, and 14.2 percent, respectively, based on preliminary 2022 U.S. EEO-1 data. Fifty-two percent of the Executive Committee were women or from diverse racial and ethnic backgrounds (based on self-identified characteristics). The company regularly reviews compensation practices to ensure fairness across genders globally and across races and ethnicities in the U.S., considering factors such as role, level, tenure, performance, and geography. After adjustments for inconsistencies, the company maintained 100 percent pay equity in 2022 globally for genders and across races and ethnicities in the U.S. The executive officers as of February 10, 2023, are listed in alphabetical order, with no family relationships among them and no appointments based on arrangements with others. American Express competes globally in the payments industry with card networks, issuers, acquirers, paper-based transactions, bank transfers, and emerging alternative payment and financing mechanisms such as digital wallets, open banking, buy now, pay later products, real-time settlement systems, financial technology companies, digital currencies, blockchain, prepaid systems, and gift cards. As a card issuer, it competes with financial institutions offering general-purpose credit and debit cards, private label card issuers, mobile wallet providers, and companies offering credit. It faces intense competition in the premium segment and for cobrand relationships, as well as for partners and differentiated offerings like airport lounge access. The company competes with other global card networks, including China UnionPay, Visa, Mastercard, JCB, Discover, and Diners Club International (owned by Discover), and is the fourth largest general-purpose card network globally by purchase volume. Other companies, including merchant acquirers, processors, and digital platforms like Alipay, PayPal, and Venmo, as well as regional networks like the National Payments Corporation of India, perform similar activities. Key competitive factors include product and service features, brand reputation, customer spending and credit performance, merchant acceptance, value proposition attractiveness, availability of alternative payment and financing options, marketing effectiveness, innovation speed, expense management tools, and data capabilities, particularly for business customers, and the security of cardholder, merchant, and network partner information. The rapid growth of alternative payment mechanisms, including financial services integration and closed-loop loyalty features, presents ongoing competitive challenges. Additionally, the company faces significant government regulation and supervision worldwide, with substantial compliance costs, and regulatory scrutiny, high expectations, and unpredictable enforcement environments.

Results may materially suffer due to substantial and increasingly intense global competition in the payments industry, as discussed in the “Risk Factors” section, and the business is subject to comprehensive government regulation and supervision, which could materially adversely affect operations and financial condition. Legal proceedings related to provisions in merchant contracts—such as non-discrimination and honor-all-cards—could have a material adverse effect on the business, leading to additional litigation or arbitrations, changes to merchant agreements or business practices, substantial monetary damages, and reputational harm. The Company, TRS, and its U.S. bank subsidiary, American Express National Bank (AENB), are subject to extensive federal and state banking laws, regulations, and policies, including oversight by the Federal Reserve, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Both the Company and TRS are consolidatedly supervised by the Federal Reserve, with AENB under OCC supervision. The Company and TRS have elected financial holding company status, which allows broader financial activities, but must maintain eligibility requirements, including being “well capitalized” and “well managed,” and AENB receiving a “satisfactory” CRA rating. The Company and its subsidiaries are prohibited from engaging in practices deemed unsafe or unsound by regulators, who have discretion in determining safe and sound operations. Acquisitions and investments are subject to regulatory review and approval by the Federal Reserve and OCC, with broad discretion in evaluations. The Company is subject to U.S. federal bank regulatory rules that categorize bank holding companies based on risk indicators, placing the Company in Category IV. As a Category IV firm, it is not subject to advanced approaches capital requirements and must maintain minimum capital ratios of 4.5% CET1, 6.0% Tier 1, and 8.0% Total capital to risk-weighted assets. The Company is subject to a dynamic stress capital buffer (SCB) of 2.5% CET1 capital, effective from October 1 each year, increasing the effective minimum ratios to 7.0% CET1, 8.5% Tier 1, and 10.5% Total capital. AENB is subject to a static 2.5% capital conservation buffer. The Company must maintain a leverage ratio of at least 4.0%. Liquidity requirements under the Federal Reserve’s enhanced prudential standards include a liquidity buffer and a minimum liquidity coverage ratio (LCR), but Category IV firms with less than $50 billion in weighted short-term wholesale funding, like the Company, are not subject to specific LCR or net stable funding ratio (NSFR) requirements. The Company participates in supervisory stress testing every other year, with the most recent test in 2022, and must submit an annual capital plan by April 5. The SCB based on stress tests is recalculated every other year, and the firm may elect to participate in an “off year” to receive an updated SCB. Capital distributions, including dividends and share repurchases, are limited if capital ratios fall below minimums or if the capital plan is resubmitted. AENB’s ability to pay dividends to TRS is restricted by law and requires approval from the OCC if not paid from recent earnings or if it would breach capital adequacy. The Federal Deposit Insurance Act (FDIA) imposes progressive restrictions on institutions based on capital categories, with AENB required to maintain CET1, Tier 1, Total capital, and Tier 1 leverage ratios of at least 6.5%, 8.0%, 10.0%, and 5.0%, respectively, to be considered “well capitalized.” AENB may be prohibited from accepting brokered deposits or offering interest rates above prevailing market rates unless well capitalized or adequately capitalized with a waiver. The Company is not required to submit a holding company resolution plan, but AENB must submit a resolution plan every three years, with the most recent submission in December 2022. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important institution in the event of default and systemic risk, with significant differences from the U.S. Bankruptcy Code, including the FDIC’s authority to disregard creditor claim priorities.

AENB is required to prepare and submit a separate resolution plan to the FDIC to enable the FDIC, as receiver, to effectively resolve the institution under the FDIA in the event of failure. Under the FDIC’s rule and its June 2021 statement, insured depository institutions with $100 billion or more in assets—such as AENB—are required to submit resolution plans on a three-year cycle, and AENB submitted its most recent resolution plan in December 2022 as required. The Company could become subject to the Orderly Liquidation Authority (OLA), under which the Treasury Secretary may appoint the FDIC as receiver to liquidate a systemically important financial institution if the Company is in danger of default and poses a systemic risk to U.S. financial stability. Under the OLA, the FDIC has broad powers as receiver, including the ability to disregard the strict priority of creditor claims in limited circumstances, use an administrative claims procedure instead of judicial proceedings, and transfer claims to a “bridge” entity. The FDIC has developed a “single point of entry” (SPOE) strategy under OLA, whereby the FDIC would transfer AENB’s assets—including shares of its operating subsidiaries—and potentially limited liabilities to a “bridge” holding company; use the failed company’s resources to recapitalize its subsidiaries; and satisfy unsecured creditor claims and other claimants by delivering securities from new financial companies emerging from the bridge entity. Under this strategy, management of the failed holding company would be replaced, and shareholders and creditors would bear the losses. If the FDIC is appointed conservator or receiver of AENB, it has the power to transfer any of AENB’s assets or liabilities to a new obligor without creditor approval, enforce contractual terms, or repudiate or disaffirm contracts or leases deemed burdensome by the FDIC. Additionally, claims of U.S. deposit holders and certain administrative expenses of the FDIC would be prioritized over other general unsecured claims, including those of debt holders and depositors in non-U.S. offices, meaning such non-U.S. depositors could receive substantially less or nothing compared to U.S. office depositors. The Company is required to act as a source of financial and managerial strength to its U.S. bank subsidiary, AENB, and may be required to commit capital or financial resources to support AENB even when it would otherwise not do so. Capital loans to AENB are subordinate to deposits and certain other indebtedness of AENB, and in the event of the Company’s bankruptcy, any commitment to a federal banking regulator to maintain AENB’s capital would be assumed by the bankruptcy trustee and given priority of payment. Certain transactions between AENB and its affiliates—including the Company, TRS, and their subsidiaries—are subject to quantitative and qualitative limitations, collateral requirements, and other restrictions under statute and regulation and must generally be made on an arm’s-length basis. AENB accepts deposits insured by the FDIC up to applicable limits, and the FDIC may terminate such insurance if AENB engages in unsafe or unsound practices, is in an unsafe or unsound condition, or violates applicable laws, regulations, rules, orders, or conditions. There is no known practice, condition, or violation at AENB that would lead to termination of deposit insurance. The FDIC’s deposit insurance fund is funded by assessments on insured institutions, including AENB, which are subject to adjustment by the FDIC. AENB is subject to the Community Reinvestment Act (CRA), which imposes affirmative, ongoing obligations to meet the credit needs of local communities, including low- and moderate-income neighborhoods, consistent with safe and sound operations. In May 2022, federal banking agencies issued a joint notice of proposed rulemaking proposing revisions to CRA regulations, including changes to assessment areas, evaluation frameworks, performance standards, definitions of community development activities, and data collection and reporting. The U.S. banking agencies have increased their focus on climate risk-related supervision; on December 16, 2021, the OCC issued for public comment proposed “Principles for Climate-Related Financial Risk Management for Large Banks,” which apply to OCC-regulated institutions with over $100 billion in total consolidated assets, such as AENB, and cover governance, policies, strategic planning, risk management, data and reporting, and scenario analysis. The principles also offer guidance on incorporating climate risks into traditional risk categories. On March 30, 2022, and December 2, 2022, the FDIC and the Federal Reserve, respectively, issued for public comment similar draft principles for financial institutions with over $100 billion in assets under their supervision, including the Company. It is too early to determine what regulations or policies may be adopted or applied, and the potential impact on the Company and AENB remains uncertain. The Company’s consumer-oriented activities are regulated in the U.S. and internationally; in the U.S., the CFPB supervises and examines marketing, sale, and servicing of consumer financial products and enforces federal consumer financial laws, including preventing “unfair, deceptive, or abusive” practices, collecting fines, requiring restitution, engaging in consumer education, tracking complaints, requesting data, and promoting access to underserved consumers. U.S. state laws also impose significant consumer credit protection, disclosure, and other requirements, some of which are more stringent than federal laws. Federal law also regulates abusive debt collection practices, which can affect the Company’s ability to collect amounts owed and subject it to regulatory scrutiny. On February 1, 2023, the CFPB issued a proposed rule to lower the safe harbor amount for late fees considered “reasonable and proportional” to costs incurred by credit card issuers, eliminate annual inflation adjustments, and prohibit late fees above 25% of the consumer’s required minimum payment; if adopted, this rule is not expected to become effective before 2024. The Company is also subject to “money transmitter” or “sale of check” laws in most U.S. states, unclaimed and abandoned property laws requiring payment of face amounts of uncashed Travelers Cheques or unredeemed prepaid cards after a specified period, and insurance laws in the U.S. and other countries where it offers insurance services. Outside the U.S., regulators focus on consumer protection (e.g., EU, UK, Canada) and responsible lending (e.g., Australia, Mexico, New Zealand, Singapore), with increasing emphasis on customer outcomes rather than compliance. Regulators are placing greater emphasis on firms’ compliance, risk, and control frameworks, particularly in systems and controls for identifying and resolving issues. In various jurisdictions, legislators and regulators have focused on card network operations, including enforcement actions, legislation, and regulations affecting interchange fees, merchant card acceptance, and pricing, and establishing ongoing oversight of payment systems. Regulation of interchange fees has negatively impacted and may continue to negatively impact the Company’s discount revenue due to downward pressure on merchant discount rates from reduced competitor pricing under interchange fee caps. The Company has exited its network businesses in the EU and Australia due to regulation in those jurisdictions. There is uncertainty regarding when or how interchange fee caps and other provisions of EU payments legislation might apply in cobrand partnerships and agent arrangements in the EU, and differing regulatory interpretations could lead to regulatory action, penalties, or the loss of existing cobrand and agent relationships. In certain EU Member States and Australia, merchants are permitted by law to surcharge card purchases. In the U.S., laws prohibiting surcharging have been overturned, and some states have passed or are considering surcharging laws. Effective October 6, 2022, merchants in Canada (excluding Quebec) are permitted to surcharge credit card purchases up to a maximum of 2.4%, resulting from a litigation settlement with Visa and Mastercard. Surcharging is an adverse customer experience and could materially harm the Company, especially if it disproportionately affects credit card usage or card usage generally, its Card Members, or its business. Other steering or differential acceptance practices permitted by regulation in some jurisdictions could also have a material adverse effect. In some countries, governments require international card networks to be locally licensed or to localize operations; for example, India’s Reserve Bank of India, under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, mandated local storage of payment data and imposed restrictions on American Express Banking Corp. in 2021, which were lifted in August 2022 after significant investment in technology, infrastructure, and resources to comply. The development and enforcement of such laws may adversely affect the Company’s ability to compete and maintain its global network. Regulatory and legislative activity in privacy, data protection, data governance, information, and cyber security continues to increase worldwide. The Company has established and maintains policies and a governance framework to comply with applicable laws and meet evolving customer and industry expectations. Regulators are increasingly focused on ensuring that privacy, data protection, cyber security policies and practices adequately inform customers about data collection, use, sharing, and security, provide them with choices, and appropriately safeguard personal information and account access. Regulators also emphasize data management, resiliency, business continuity, and third-party risk management. In the U.S., certain businesses are subject to the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLBA) and its regulations, which limit sharing of consumers’ nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties and require a written comprehensive information security program appropriate to the business size, complexity, and sensitivity of customer data. The Company has expanded privacy rights for California residents under the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 and the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020. Various U.S. regulators, states, and territories are considering or have adopted privacy or cyber security laws that may be more stringent or expansive than federal requirements. The Company is also subject to privacy, data protection, data governance, and cyber security laws in other countries, including the EU, Australia, Canada, China, Japan, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Mexico, Singapore, Thailand, and the UK, some of which are more stringent or expansive than U.S. laws and may conflict with each other. Some jurisdictions impose onerous requirements for transferring personal data to other jurisdictions, while others require in-country data processing or storage. Compliance increases technology, administrative, and other costs, limits the ability to optimize closed-loop data, and may require local technology services. Some laws also require broader access to data and intellectual property by foreign governments or third parties. Data breach and operational outage notification laws, as well as regulatory activities promoting such notifications and resiliency, business continuity, and third-party risk management, are becoming more prevalent in jurisdictions outside the U.S. In Europe, the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) imposes legal and compliance obligations on companies processing personal data of individuals in the EU, regardless of location, with potential fines up to 4% of total worldwide annual revenue. The GDPR requires prompt notification of data breaches to affected individuals and supervisory authorities. The UK GDPR mirrors the GDPR’s compliance requirements and fine structure. In October 2022, an Executive Order, together with U.S. Department of Justice regulations, was signed to implement a new data privacy framework for cross-border transfers of EU personal data to the U.S. The Company is also subject to significant supervision and an increasingly stringent enforcement environment regarding compliance with anti-money laundering (AML), countering the financing of terrorism (CFT), economic sanctions, and anti-corruption laws. Failure to maintain adequate AML/CFT, sanctions, and anti-corruption programs and procedures could result in material financial, legal, and reputational consequences. In the U.S., AML/CFT requirements primarily stem from the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act and regulations issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury (Bank Secrecy Act), as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), enacted in January 2021, amended the Bank Secrecy Act and aims to comprehensively reform and modernize U.S. AML/CFT laws, with many statutory provisions requiring additional rulemakings, reports, and measures, the effects of which are not yet known. In Europe, AML/CFT requirements are largely derived from countries transposing the 5th and 6th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (and earlier directives) into local laws.

We are subject to a significant number of anti-money laundering and counterfinancing of terrorism (AML/CFT) laws and regulations globally. In the United States, the majority of AML/CFT requirements stem from the Currency and Foreign Transactions Reporting Act and the regulations issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury, collectively known as the Bank Secrecy Act, as amended by the USA PATRIOT Act of 2001. The Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020 (AMLA), enacted in January 2021, amended the Bank Secrecy Act and aims to comprehensively reform and modernize U.S. AML/CFT laws. Many of its statutory provisions will require additional rulemakings, reports, and other measures, the effects of which are not yet known. In Europe, AML/CFT requirements arise primarily from countries transposing the 5th and 6th EU Anti-Money Laundering Directives (and earlier directives) into local laws and regulations. Numerous other countries, including Argentina, Australia, Canada, India, Mexico, New Zealand, and Russia, have enacted or proposed new or enhanced AML/CFT legislation applicable to American Express. These laws and regulations require us to establish AML/CFT programs that meet certain standards, including expanded reporting—particularly on suspicious transactions—and enhanced information gathering and recordkeeping. Our AML/CFT programs have faced heightened scrutiny in some countries, including certain EU Member States. Any errors, failures, or delays in complying with AML/CFT laws, perceived deficiencies in our programs, or an association of our business with money laundering, terrorist financing, tax fraud, or other illicit activity can lead to significant supervisory, criminal, and civil proceedings and lawsuits, resulting in substantial penalties, forfeiture of assets, loss of licenses, restrictions on business activities, or other enforcement actions. We are also subject to economic sanctions imposed by national governments and international bodies such as the United Nations and the EU, targeting individuals, entities, vessels, governments, and countries that threaten their interests or violate international norms. These sanctions are used to advance foreign policy goals such as conflict resolution, counterterrorism, counternarcotics, and promotion of democracy and human rights. Failure to comply can result in serious legal and reputational consequences, including criminal penalties. The United States has imposed sanctions affecting transactions with designated foreign countries, nationals, and others, prohibiting U.S. persons from engaging with individuals or entities listed as “Specially Designated Nationals” (such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers) without a license or authorization. These prohibitions are administered by the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), which prohibits financial transactions with such entities, requires the blocking of assets in which they have an interest, and bans transfers of property subject to U.S. jurisdiction. Blocked assets, such as property or bank deposits, cannot be paid out, withdrawn, set off, or transferred without an OFAC license. We maintain a global sanctions compliance program to meet the requirements of applicable sanctions regimes. We are also subject to complex anti-corruption laws, including the U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA), the UK Bribery Act, and other laws that prohibit improper payments. The FCPA makes it illegal to offer or provide anything of value to foreign government officials, political parties, or political party officials to obtain or retain business or an improper advantage. It also requires strict compliance with accounting and internal controls. The UK Bribery Act prohibits commercial bribery and receipt of bribes and makes it a corporate offense to fail to prevent bribery by an associated person, in addition to prohibiting improper payments to foreign government officials. Failure by us or our colleagues, contractors, or agents to comply with the FCPA, the UK Bribery Act, or similar laws can result in investigations, prosecutions, and potentially severe criminal and civil penalties. Our compensation practices are overseen by the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC). Federal banking regulators’ guidance on sound incentive compensation practices outlines three key principles: (1) incentives should appropriately balance risk and financial results without encouraging imprudent risk-taking, (2) incentive plans must be compatible with effective internal controls and risk management, and (3) they must be supported by strong corporate governance, including active and effective oversight by the board of directors. Deficiencies in our compensation practices identified by regulators may be incorporated into our supervisory ratings, affecting our ability to make acquisitions or perform other actions. Enforcement actions may be taken if our incentive compensation arrangements or related risk-management or governance processes are found to pose a risk to our safety and soundness and we have not taken prompt and effective corrective measures. The Dodd-Frank Act requires U.S. financial regulators, including the Federal Reserve and the SEC, to adopt rules on incentive-based payment arrangements for entities with at least $1 billion in total assets. In 2016, the federal banking regulators, the SEC, the Federal Housing Finance Agency, and the National Credit Union Administration proposed revised rules on incentive-based compensation practices, which have not yet been finalized. If adopted in a form similar to the proposal, these rules would impose limitations on how we structure compensation for our colleagues, potentially harming our ability to hire, retain, and motivate key personnel. In October 2022, the SEC adopted a new rule requiring national securities exchanges to mandate policies that require the recovery of excess incentive-based compensation paid to current or former executive officers in the case of a restatement of previously issued financial statements, and require listed issuers to disclose any recovery analysis triggered by such restatements. Our business as a whole has not experienced significant seasonal fluctuations, although network volumes are moderately higher in the fourth quarter than in other quarters, leading to moderately higher Card Member loans and receivables during that period. The average discount rate tends to be slightly lower in the fourth quarter due to a higher level of retail-related billed business. Our business is subject to the effects of geopolitical conditions, weather, natural disasters, and other catastrophic events. We face intense competition for partner relationships, which could lead to loss or renegotiation of agreements, materially affecting our business and operations. We have partnered with Delta, Marriott, Hilton, British Airways, and many other global businesses to offer cobranded cards and benefits through our Membership Rewards program. All cobrand portfolios collectively accounted for approximately 18 percent of our worldwide network volumes as of December 31, 2022, and card member loans related to these portfolios accounted for about 36 percent of our worldwide card member loans at that date. Cobrand arrangements typically last between five and ten years and terminate at the end of the term unless renewed or extended, or early due to default. We face the risk of losing partner relationships, even after significant investment, and may choose not to renew certain arrangements. Termination of cobrand partnerships could lead to a decline in network volumes and increased card member attrition, and some arrangements allow the cobrand partner to purchase or designate a third party to purchase the loans generated, resulting in loss of card accounts and a significant reduction in outstanding card member loans. We regularly seek to extend or renew these arrangements, but face risks of renegotiating on less favorable terms or being unable to secure acceptable terms due to rising competition. We make payments to cobrand partners based on Card Member spending, rewards earned, and in some cases, the number of accounts acquired and retained, with payments increasing, particularly in the U.S., due to heightened competition. Loss of exclusivity, complete termination of partnerships—such as the end of the relationship with Costco in the U.S. in 2016 or American Airlines’ withdrawal from the Airport Club Access program in 2014—or renegotiation with worse terms could materially harm our business. Publicity surrounding such losses could damage our reputation, making it harder to attract and retain card members and merchants and weakening our negotiating power with current and prospective partners. Business partner arrangements represent a significant portion of our operations, exposing us to risks such as reputational issues, business slowdowns, bankruptcies, liquidations, restructurings, and consolidations, as well as potential obligations to make payments upon performance shortfalls or revenue declines. The company’s balance sheet management objectives include maintaining a solid and flexible equity capital profile, a broad, deep, and diverse set of funding sources, and liquidity programs to meet future financing obligations and business requirements for at least twelve months in the event of a substantial weakening in economic conditions. The company manages its balance sheet in response to market volatility. Capital is allocated to growing businesses with a return on risk-adjusted equity exceeding costs to generate shareholder value. The company retains capital from net income and stock option exercises to maintain a strong balance sheet, support future growth, and distribute excess capital through dividends and share repurchases. The consolidated capital position is determined through the Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process, considering business activities, marketplace conditions, and regulatory or shareholder expectations. As a bank holding company, it is subject to U.S. federal banking agency regulations, including Federal Reserve capital adequacy guidelines. Failure to maintain minimum regulatory capital levels at American Express or American Express National Bank (AENB) could affect its financial holding company status and lead to regulatory actions limiting operations. The company seeks to maintain capital levels and ratios above minimum regulatory requirements, specifically within a 10 to 11 percent target range for Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) risk-based capital ratio. Capital can be shifted across businesses as needed, such as infusing additional capital into subsidiaries to meet debt ratings and regulatory requirements, which may affect parent or subsidiary capital and liquidity positions. Capital ratios are reported using Basel III definitions and the standardized approach for risk-weighted assets. As of December 31, 2022, the regulatory risk-based capital and leverage ratios were: Common Equity Tier 1 at 10.3% for American Express Company and 11.3% for AENB; Tier 1 at 11.1% and 11.3%; Total at 12.8% and 13.2%; Tier 1 Leverage at 9.9% and 9.7%. The minimum requirements include the stress capital buffer (SCB) for American Express Company and the capital conservation buffer for AENB. American Express Company’s regulatory risk-based capital components and risk-weighted assets as of December 31, 2022, were: Common Equity Tier 1 $20.0 billion, Tier 1 Capital $21.6 billion, Tier 2 Capital $3.3 billion, Total Capital $24.9 billion, and Risk-Weighted Assets $194.4 billion. Average total assets for the Tier 1 Leverage Ratio were $218.6 billion. Risk-Weighted Assets are calculated using a Federal Reserve formula that weights assets by risk, including off-balance sheet items converted to balance sheet equivalents using risk conversion factors. Common Equity Tier 1 Risk-Based Capital Ratio is calculated as CET1 capital divided by risk-weighted assets, with CET1 capital adjusted for ineligible goodwill, intangible assets, deferred tax assets, and CECL final rules. Tier 1 Risk-Based Capital Ratio is calculated as Tier 1 capital divided by risk-weighted assets, with Tier 1 capital including CET1 capital, preferred shares, and third-party non-controlling interests, adjusted for insurance subsidiary capital. The minimum Tier 1 ratio is 1.5% higher than CET1. The company has $1.6 billion in preferred shares to meet Tier 1 capital requirements. Total Risk-Based Capital Ratio is calculated as (Tier 1 + Tier 2) capital divided by risk-weighted assets, with Tier 2 capital including the reserve for loan and receivable credit losses (limited to 1.25% of risk-weighted assets) and $870 million in eligible subordinated notes, including $750 million issued in May 2022 and $120 million remaining from $600 million issued in December 2014. Tier 1 Leverage Ratio is calculated as Tier 1 capital divided by average total consolidated assets for the most recent quarter. The company uses an Enterprise-wide Risk Management (ERM) program to identify, aggregate, monitor, measure, report, and manage risks, defining risk appetite, governance, culture, and capabilities, with the Chief Risk Officer leading its implementation. Risk management is overseen by the Board of Directors through three committees: the Risk Committee, the Audit and Compliance Committee, and the Compensation and Benefits Committee, each composed entirely of independent directors and meeting regularly with senior management. The Risk Committee oversees the ERM framework, approves the ERM policy, and reviews risk appetite across credit, operational, compliance, reputational, market, funding, liquidity, model, strategic, business, country, and environmental, social, and governance risks, including limits and escalation triggers. It reviews the appointment, performance, and compensation of the Chief Risk Officer and monitors risk profile against tolerances, compliance with regulatory capital and liquidity standards, and CCAR submissions. The Audit and Compliance Committee reviews compliance policies, including the Compliance Risk Tolerance Statement, the effectiveness of the Corporate-wide Compliance Risk Management Program, financial statement integrity, internal and external auditing, and internal audit performance and independence. It approves the Chief Audit Executive’s appointment, performance, and compensation, and reviews the annual audit plan, charter, policies, budget, staffing, and risk assessment methodology. The Compensation and Benefits Committee works with the Chief Risk Officer to balance risk with business incentives, sets risk goals, reviews business unit risk profiles, and uses a risk-balanced incentive framework to determine bonus pools and senior executive compensation. The Enterprise Risk Management Committee (ERMC), chaired by the Chief Risk Officer, is the highest-level management committee overseeing firm-wide risks, maintaining the enterprise-wide risk appetite framework, monitoring compliance with limits, and overseeing risk policy implementation. The Asset Liability Committee, chaired by the Chief Financial Officer, manages capital, funding, liquidity, investment, market risk, and asset/liability activities in compliance with policies and regulations. The company follows a “three lines of defense” approach: the first line includes the Chief Executive Officer, business unit presidents, and Chief Financial Officer who initiate risk-taking; the second line includes the Chief Risk Officer, Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Operational Risk Officer, and control groups who oversee risk-taking; the third line is the Internal Audit Group, which provides independent assessments of the first and second lines. Credit risk is defined as loss due to default or changes in credit quality and is divided into individual and institutional categories. Individual credit risk arises from consumer and small business charge cards, credit cards, and term loans, involving millions of customers across geographies and industries, with risk generally correlated to economic trends like unemployment and GDP growth. Business unit leaders and Chief Credit Officers manage this risk, guided by the Individual Credit Risk Committee (ICRC), which ensures compliance with ERMC guidelines and escalates issues as needed. Sophisticated proprietary scoring and decision-making models using spending, payment history, and credit bureau data support credit risk management. Institutional credit risk arises in CS, ICS, GMNS, investment, and liquidity activities, characterized by lower loss frequency but higher severity, influenced by both economic conditions and client-specific events. Business units are supported by Chief Credit Officers guided by the Institutional Risk Management Committee (IRMC), which implements the Institutional Credit Risk Management Policy, makes investment decisions, ensures underwriting standards, monitors exposures, and determines risk mitigation actions, formally reviews large exposures, and provides guidance to optimize risk-adjusted returns. A centralized risk rating unit assesses institutional obligors. The company has significant cobrand, rewards, merchant acceptance, and corporate payments arrangements with airlines, with Delta being the largest partner, including an exclusive cobrand credit card partnership and Membership Rewards redemption. The ERM program evaluates airline and travel industry risks, including cruise lines, travel agencies, and tour operators. Debt exposure is monitored for sovereign and non-sovereign customers and counterparties by geographic region and economic sector, with a focus on credit deterioration due to economic and fiscal weaknesses; as of December 31, 2022, gross credit exposures to high-risk countries were considered individually and collectively not material. Operational risk is defined as loss due to inadequate processes, people, systems, or external environment impacts, including regulatory non-compliance and third-party relationships. A comprehensive operational risk framework, approved by the ERMC, includes operational risk event capture, a project office for issue management, key risk indicators, and process and entity-level risk assessments. The Operational Risk Management Committee (ORMC), chaired by the Chief Operational Risk Officer, coordinates risk assessments and controls, oversees preventive and responsive efforts by Operational Excellence teams, and requires root cause analysis, impact assessment (operational, financial, brand, regulatory, legal), and resolution plans. Information and cyber security risk is defined as the risk of a security incident impacting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of customer, colleague, or proprietary information. The program uses advanced technology, a trained team, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, with controls for identification, protection, detection, response, and recovery. Information technology risk is the risk of events compromising processing, stability, capacity, performance, or resilience of IT systems, leading to financial, reputational, or regulatory impacts. The company manages IT risk through policies, procedures, governance, and controls to preserve system confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Privacy risk is the risk of financial loss, reputational damage, or legal action from violating laws, regulations, contractual obligations, or privacy policies in processing personal data. The Global Privacy Policy establishes data protection principles, and the Privacy Risk Management Committee, chaired by the Chief Privacy Officer and a sub-committee of the ORMC, provides oversight. Data management and governance risk is the risk of financial, reputational, or regulatory impacts from inadequate data governance or management practices affecting data accuracy, completeness, timeliness, comprehensiveness, or usability. The Enterprise Data Governance Policy defines in-scope critical data and lifecycle management requirements, approved by the ERMC. The Enterprise Data Committee, chaired by the Chief Data Officer and a sub-committee of the ERMC, provides governance and oversight. Third party risk is the risk from relationships with third parties or their subcontractors leading to unexpected outcomes or deviations. The Third Party Management Policy, approved by the Risk Committee and ERMC, sets procurement, risk management, and contracting frameworks, and the Third Party Lifecycle Management program guides identification, measurement, monitoring, and reporting of third-party risk throughout the relationship lifecycle. Conduct risk is the risk that colleagues fail to fulfill responsibilities in accordance with the Code of Conduct, policies, values, or laws, potentially increasing reputational risk. The Conduct Risk Management Policy, approved by the ERMC, requires annual risk assessments, preventive and detective controls, colleague training, and timely escalation of conduct issues, with consequence management for substantiated misconduct. The Conduct Risk Committee oversees conduct risk and escalates matters to the ERMC as appropriate. Compliance risk is the risk of legal or reputational harm, fines, penalties, or sanctions due to non-compliance with laws, regulations, internal policies, or ethical standards. The Global Compliance and Ethics organization manages compliance risk through assessment, control, monitoring, measuring, and reporting. The Compliance Risk Management Committee (CRMC), chaired by the Chief Compliance Officer, identifies, evaluates, manages, and escalates compliance risks and has a dual reporting relationship to the ERMC and the Audit and Compliance Committee. The company has a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering program that monitors suspicious activity and includes an independent risk assessment of its rules, with the Internal Audit Group reviewing processes for consistency.

We define compliance risk as the risk of legal or reputational harm, fines, monetary penalties, and other sanctions arising from non-compliance with applicable laws and regulations, internal policies, procedures, and ethical standards. Our Global Compliance and Ethics organization oversees the corporate-wide Compliance Risk Management Program, which involves assessing, controlling, monitoring, measuring, and reporting legal and regulatory risks. The Compliance Risk Management Committee (CRMC), chaired by the Chief Compliance Officer, identifies, evaluates, manages, and escalates compliance risks and maintains a dual reporting relationship with both the ERMC and the Audit and Compliance Committee. We maintain a comprehensive Anti-Money Laundering program that monitors and reports suspicious activity to government authorities and includes an independent risk assessment of the rules used by the team; the Internal Audit Group reviews processes for consistency with regulatory guidance. Reputational risk is defined as the risk of negative stakeholder reactions to our products, services, client and partner relationships, business activities, policies, management, workplace culture, or responses to unexpected events, which could lead to sustained media coverage, revenue or investment decline, talent attrition, litigation, or regulatory scrutiny. We view protecting our reputation for excellent customer service, trust, security, and integrity as central to our vision of delivering the world’s best customer experience and long-term success. Business leaders are responsible for considering reputational risks in business activities and strategies and ensuring relevant subject matter experts are engaged. The ERMC ensures reputational risk considerations are included in subordinate risk policies and committees and properly reflected in decisions escalated to it. Market risk is defined as the risk to earnings or asset and liability values from movements in market prices, including interest rate risk—due to changes in the relationship between interest rates on assets (such as loans, receivables, and investment securities) and liabilities (such as debt and deposits)—and foreign exchange risk from transactions, funding, investments, and earnings in currencies other than the U.S. dollar. Market risk policies, approved by the ERMC, Asset Liability Committee, or Market Risk Management Committee, establish quantitative limits and escalation triggers and are managed by the Market Risk Management Committee. The Market Risk Oversight Officer provides independent risk assessment and oversight of market risk and Asset Liability Management policies and regulatory compliance, guided by policies on derivatives, funding, liquidity, and investments. Actual net interest income changes may differ due to timing, rate movements, and other factors. Foreign exchange risk arises from four sources: Card Member spending in non-billing currencies, cross-currency transactions and balances, cross-currency investing (e.g., foreign subsidiary equity), and foreign currency revenues and expenses. Funding and liquidity risk is defined as our inability to meet financial and business obligations at reasonable cost as they become due. Our Board-approved Liquidity Risk Policy governs liquidity risk management. The Funding and Liquidity Committee manages this risk by maintaining access to a diverse set of cash, readily-marketable securities, and contingent liquidity sources to meet business requirements and financing obligations for at least twelve months under stressed economic conditions. The committee reviews cash and financing forecasts, approves funding plans under normal and stressed conditions, establishes liquidity guidelines, and monitors positions to determine actions. Funding and liquidity risk is managed at both the consolidated and subsidiary levels. Model risk is defined as the risk of adverse outcomes—such as financial loss, poor decision-making, reputational damage, or customer harm—from decisions based on incorrect or misused model outputs. The Enterprise-Wide Model Risk Policy, approved by the ERMC, establishes a comprehensive framework including procedures for model development, independent validation, risk reporting, and change management to minimize errors in methodology, outputs, and misuse. Ongoing performance assessments and deficiencies are addressed promptly. Artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) models are used in various business applications, and extensive reviews and testing are conducted to reduce adverse consequences. Strategic and business risk is defined as the risk of failing to achieve business objectives due to poor strategic decisions, including mergers, acquisitions, divestitures, poor implementation, or declining demand. Strategic decisions are reviewed and approved by business leaders and committees and must align with company policies. Risk controls are embedded in these processes, and existing product performance is periodically reviewed by committees and leaders. Mergers, acquisitions, and divestitures require Executive Committee due diligence, a comprehensive risk assessment by operational, market, credit, and oversight leaders provided to the Chief Risk Officer, and approval by the Chief Risk Officer or appropriate risk committees. All new and material product or service changes are reviewed and approved by the New Products Committee and relevant credit or risk committees. Country risk is defined as the risk from economic, social, or political conditions in a country that could adversely affect us, primarily through greater credit losses, increased operational or market risk, or inability to repatriate capital. Country risk is managed as part of normal business operations, with policies and procedures setting escalation thresholds to control exposure and monitor conditions in countries where we operate. Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) and climate-related risk includes risks from the transition to a low-carbon economy—such as policy, legal, technological, market, and reputational risks—and physical impacts of climate change, such as extreme weather events and long-term climate shifts. These risks can affect customers, operations, suppliers, and business and are interconnected across all risk types, potentially manifesting as credit, operational, market, or liquidity risks. Climate-related risk is currently identified as an “emerging risk” within our risk governance framework, and we are conducting a risk identification process to assess its meaningfulness and measurability. Critical accounting estimates include reserves for Card Member credit losses, which represent our best estimate of expected credit losses in the outstanding portfolio of loans and receivables as of the balance sheet date. The Current Expected Credit Loss (CECL) methodology, effective January 1, 2020, requires estimating lifetime expected credit losses using historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period) beyond the balance sheet date. We use a combination of statistical models and analysis to determine quantitative and qualitative components of reserves, involving significant judgment. Key judgments include selecting the appropriate R&S Period (approximately three years), modeling probability of default and exposure at default, and incorporating economic conditions. For revolving loans, future payments are allocated first to interest and fees, then to estimated higher minimum payments due to future spend, and finally to the remaining balance. For non-revolving receivables, balances are assumed to be paid or written off within 180 days past due. The R&S Period is the maximum time beyond the balance sheet date over which expected credit losses can be reasonably estimated using available information and forecasts. Beyond this period, long-term average loss rates are applied. The R&S Period includes assumptions about current and future economic conditions, incorporating multiple macroeconomic scenarios from an independent third party. Estimated credit losses from each scenario are reviewed and weighted based on management judgment. A 10 percentage point shift from a baseline to a pessimistic downside scenario as of December 31, 2022, increases estimated credit losses by approximately $120 million. This sensitivity analysis is hypothetical and does not reflect management’s judgment on scenario weighting or other adjustments, nor does it account for qualitative reserve components. Refer to Note 3 for details on macroeconomic scenario variables. The process of estimating reserves requires significant judgment, and actual losses may differ materially from estimates, resulting in higher or lower future provisions. The liability for Membership Rewards represents our best estimate of the cost of points expected to be redeemed by Card Members in the future. This liability is influenced by enrollment levels, attrition, points earned and redeemed, and redemption costs. It is estimated using the redemption rate ratio (URR) and weighted average cost (WAC) per point, applied to current enrollees. The URR is estimated using statistical and actuarial models based on historical redemption trends.

Membership Rewards points are redeemable for a wide range of rewards, including travel, shopping, gift cards, and eligible charges, with no expiration date and no cap on the number of points a Card Member can earn. The cost of these points is driven by charge volume on enrolled cards, customer participation in the program, and contractual agreements with redemption partners. A Membership Rewards liability is recorded to reflect the best estimate of the cost of points expected to be redeemed by Card Members in the future. This liability is influenced over time by enrollment levels, attrition, points earned and redeemed, and associated redemption costs. The liability is estimated using the Ultimate Redemption Rate (URR) and the weighted average cost (WAC) per point, applied to the points of current enrollees. The URR is estimated using statistical and actuarial models based on redemption trends, card product type, enrollment tenure, card spend levels, and credit attributes. The WAC per point is derived from 12 months of redemptions and adjusted for changes in redemption costs that do not reflect future expectations or shifts in redemption patterns. The company periodically reviews its liability estimates based on changes in redemption patterns, cost per point, partner contract changes, and other factors. The estimation process involves significant judgment, and actual redemptions and costs could differ materially from estimates, affecting Membership Rewards expense. An increase in the URR by 25 basis points as of December 31, 2022, would increase the liability and expense by approximately $157 million, while a 1 basis point increase in WAC per point would increase the liability and expense by approximately $190 million. Goodwill, representing the excess of acquisition cost over fair value of assets and liabilities, is not amortized but is tested annually or when events suggest a reporting unit’s fair value is below its carrying value. The impairment test includes both qualitative and quantitative assessments; if qualitative factors indicate it is more likely than not that fair value is below carrying value, a detailed quantitative assessment follows. The quantitative test uses either the income approach (discounted cash flows based on internal forecasts and terminal values using a growth rate appropriate to current economic conditions, discounted at a cost of equity derived from a capital asset pricing model) or the market approach (applying market multiples to operating results). Significant judgment is involved in forecasting cash flows, discount rates, and market comparables, and differences from assumptions could materially affect fair value. The company is exposed to increased goodwill impairment risk if future operating results or macroeconomic conditions differ from current expectations. The company is a globally integrated payments company providing credit and charge card products, travel and lifestyle services to consumers and businesses worldwide through various channels. The Consolidated Financial Statements are prepared in accordance with U.S. GAAP, with significant intercompany transactions eliminated. Entities are consolidated if the company holds a controlling financial interest, determined by power to direct activities and obligation to absorb losses or right to receive benefits that could be significant. For entities without control but with significant influence, the equity method is used. Investments in equity securities below significant influence are recorded at cost and adjusted to fair value. Transactions in foreign currencies are converted at transaction dates, with remeasurement at period-end rates, and translation adjustments are included in accumulated other comprehensive income (loss). Accounting estimates, including reserves for credit losses, Membership Rewards liability, goodwill, and income taxes, are based on management’s assumptions and reflect best judgments. Revenue is recognized when obligations under contracts are satisfied. Discount revenue is earned from merchant payable fees for facilitating transactions, recorded at transaction time, with contract durations varying by merchant size. Net card fees are deferred and recognized on a straight-line basis over the membership period, with unamortized balances reported in Other liabilities. Service Fees and Other Revenue are included in the income statement.

Existing agreements may continue beyond their stated expiration dates until a new agreement is reached, and obligations under these agreements are satisfied over the contract term, often on a daily basis, including through the processing of Card Member transactions and the availability of the payment network. When a merchant acquirer is a third party—such as under the OptBlue program or with certain network partners—the company receives a network rate fee in settlement with that acquirer, which is individually negotiated and recorded as discount revenue at the time of the Card Member transaction. Net card fees arise from annual card membership fees, which vary by card type and number of cards per account; these fees, net of acquisition costs and a reserve for projected refunds from cancellations, are deferred and recognized on a straight-line basis over the twelve-month membership period as Net card fees in the Consolidated Statements of Income, providing stability amid short-term business or economic shifts. The unamortized net card fee balance is reported in Other liabilities on the Consolidated Balance Sheets. Service fees and other revenue include service fees from merchants and other customers, travel commissions and fees recognized when the service is performed, and delinquency and foreign currency-related fees recognized when charged to the Card Member; it also includes income (losses) from investments where the company has significant influence, accounted for under the equity method, as detailed in Note 18. Processed revenue primarily consists of network partnership revenues, including royalties, fees, and transaction facilitation fees for cards issued by network partners. As the operator of the American Express network, the company settles with merchants and third-party merchant acquirers on behalf of network card issuers, deducting the fees for accepting American Express-branded cards from the payment and recording the amount as Processed revenue at the time of the transaction. The issuer rate is individually negotiated between the issuer and the company and is recorded as contra-revenue within Processed revenue when revenue from the same customer is present, with any additional issuer rate recorded as an expense in Business development. Processed revenue also includes fees from alternative payment solutions, recognized when the service is performed. Payments made under contractual arrangements with merchants, network partners, and other customers are classified as contra-revenue, except when goods, services, or other benefits are received with a determinable and measurable fair value, in which case they are recorded as expenses. Interest on Card Member loans is calculated using the average daily balance method and recognized based on the outstanding principal under the account agreement, unless the loan is non-accrual, until the balance is paid or written off. Interest and dividends on investment securities relate primarily to performing fixed-income securities and are recognized using the effective interest method, which adjusts for premiums, discounts, fees, and other payments to ensure a constant rate of return on the outstanding balance, until securities are in default or future interest payments are unlikely. Interest on deposits with banks and other institutions is recognized as earned and primarily relates to cash placed in interest-bearing time deposits, overnight sweep accounts, and other interest-bearing demand or call accounts. Interest expense includes interest incurred to fund Card Member loans and receivables, general corporate purposes, and liquidity needs, recognized as incurred and divided into two categories: (i) deposits, primarily related to interest on customer and institutional deposits, and (ii) debt, primarily related to long-term and short-term borrowings, plus the realized impact of derivatives used to hedge interest rate risk on long-term debt. Card Member rewards are offered through charge and credit cards, including Membership Rewards, cash back, and cobrand programs. Rewards expense is recognized in the period Card Members earn rewards through spending on enrolled card products. For Membership Rewards and cash back, a liability is recorded for expected redemptions and, for Membership Rewards, the estimated cost of points earned. For cobrand, a liability is recorded based on rewards earned on spending on cobrand cards, with associated payments made to cobrand partners; the partner is responsible for providing rewards under its own loyalty program. Card Member rewards liabilities are influenced by enrollment levels, attrition, volume of points earned and redeemed, and redemption costs, with changes during the period reflected as increases or decreases in Card Member rewards expense in the Consolidated Statements of Income. Business development expense includes payments to cobrand partners, corporate client incentive payments for achieving pre-set targets, and certain payments to network partners, all generally expensed as incurred. Card Member services expense represents costs for providing value-added benefits and services to Card Members and is generally expensed as incurred. Marketing expense includes costs for advertising development and initial placement, expensed in the period the advertising first occurs, and all other marketing expenses are generally expensed as incurred. Cash and cash equivalents include cash, amounts due from banks, interest-bearing bank balances (including securities purchased under resale agreements), restricted cash, and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of 90 days or less; restricted cash primarily relates to Card Member credit balances and upcoming debt maturities of consolidated VIEs. Goodwill represents the excess of acquisition cost over the fair value of assets and liabilities acquired and is allocated to reporting units for impairment testing. A reporting unit is defined as an operating segment or a business one level below an operating segment, for which discrete financial information is regularly reviewed by the segment manager. Goodwill is evaluated annually as of June 30, or more frequently if events or circumstances indicate that the fair value of a reporting unit is more likely than not below its carrying value. Before performing the impairment assessment, a recoverability test of certain long-lived assets is conducted. The company has the option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if it is more likely than not that a reporting unit’s fair value is below its carrying value; if so, a quantitative assessment is performed. The qualitative assessment evaluates factors such as economic conditions, industry and market trends, cost factors, financial performance, and other company- or unit-specific events. If the fair value is found to be below carrying value, a quantitative assessment is conducted, which compares the reporting unit’s fair value to its carrying amount, including goodwill. If the carrying amount exceeds fair value, an impairment loss is recognized for the excess. Fair value is measured using widely accepted valuation techniques, combining the income approach (discounted cash flows) and market approach (market multiples). Discounted cash flows use internal forecasts to estimate future cash flows, discounted at the expected cost of equity derived from a capital asset pricing model, which reflects market risks and uncertainties. Market multiples apply comparable publicly traded companies’ earnings or revenue multiples to the reporting unit’s operating results. For the years ended December 31, 2022 and 2021, a qualitative assessment was performed and determined that the fair values of all reporting units exceeded their carrying values. In 2022, a quantitative goodwill impairment assessment was conducted for reporting units affected by the realignment of operating segments, and their fair values were found to exceed carrying values. The reserves for credit losses are based on the current expected credit loss (CECL) methodology, which estimates lifetime expected credit losses over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period) of approximately three years beyond the balance sheet date, incorporating historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions. The process uses models for probability of default (PD), exposure at default (EAD), and future recoveries. PD models estimate the likelihood of write-off, EAD models estimate the balance at write-off, including expected repayments based on historical payment and revolve behavior, and recovery models estimate future recoveries. Beyond the R&S Period, expected credit losses are estimated using long-term average loss rates.

The company estimates expected credit losses by incorporating historical loss experience and current and future economic conditions over a reasonable and supportable period (R&S Period), which is approximately three years beyond the balance sheet date. A reserve rate is determined through judgments combined with historical data and applied to outstanding loan or receivable balances to generate a credit loss reserve. This process uses statistically-based models that include Probability of Default (PD), Exposure at Default (EAD), and future recoveries for each month of the R&S Period. PD models estimate the likelihood of an account being written off, EAD models estimate the balance at default, accounting for expected repayments based on historical payment and revolve behavior—particularly relevant in revolving portfolios due to complex assumptions about future spend and payment patterns—and recovery models estimate amounts expected to be recovered from Card Members after default, considering time of default, time since default, and macroeconomic conditions. The company also evaluates expected recoveries for previously written-off accounts based on how long ago they were written off and future economic conditions, even if such recoveries exceed expected losses. Models are developed using historical loss data across the economic cycle and consider account-specific risk factors. Future economic conditions during the R&S Period are based on multiple macroeconomic scenarios provided by an independent third party, which management reviews periodically and weights based on uncertainty. Key variables in these scenarios include unemployment rates and real GDP growth (quarter-over-quarter, seasonally adjusted to annualized rates). Qualitative reserves are assessed to cover losses not fully captured by quantitative methods or economic assumptions, and quantitative reserves may be adjusted to address model limitations or external factors such as portfolio trends, concentrations, past due account volume, or management risk actions. Lifetime losses are evaluated at a granular level, including pooled assessments for financial assets with similar risk characteristics like past spend, remittance behavior, credit bureau scores, delinquency status, and tenure. Credit losses on accrued interest are measured and reported in the Consolidated Balance Sheets and Consolidated Statements of Income, not by reversing interest income. Separate models are used for troubled debt restructurings (TDRs), which are measured individually using a discounted cash flow model. Loans and receivables are written off when deemed uncollectible, typically after 180 days past due for pay-in-full or revolving loans and 120 days for term loans, or upon notification in cases of bankruptcy or debts owed by deceased individuals.
